title: Thermomechanical and tribological behaviour of gravity die cast A356 aluminium composites reinforced with date palm seed ash for automotive applications
abstract: Abstract Lightweight aluminium alloys remain central to the design of modern automotive engine components, yet their limited resistance to wear and thermal instability under service conditions restricts wider structural applications. In this study, date palm seed ash (DPSA), an underutilised agro-waste by-product rich in metal oxides, was introduced as a reinforcing phase into gravity die-cast A356 alloy to improve its multifunctional performance. The DPSA was synthesised by controlled calcination at 500 °C and incorporated into the molten alloy through a semi-solid compo-casting route at 0–1.0 wt% reinforcement. The cast composites were evaluated in both as-cast and T6-treated conditions using mechanical, tribological, thermal, and microstructural techniques. The introduction of DPSA resulted in measurable refinement of the aluminium matrix. T6-treatment modified the eutectic silicon phase. There were noticeable improvements in the strength, hardness, and wear resistance of the composites up to 0.75 wt% reinforcement level, beyond which particle clustering and micro-void formation led to the deterioration of these properties. The T6-treated 0.75 wt% composite recorded the best combination of properties. Thermal analyses further revealed improved oxidation resistance and a consistent reduction in the coefficient of thermal expansion with increasing DPSA content. This confirmed that low fractions of DPSA can act simultaneously as grain refiners, load-bearing particulates, and thermal stabilisers within the A356 matrix. The T6-treatment further enhanced the mechanical, thermal and tribological properties of the composites. The study showed the synergistic use of low-weight fraction DPSA reinforcement and T6 treatment to enhance the performance characteristics of gravity die-cast A356 composites for automotive applications. sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Aluminium alloys represent one of the most widely used engineering materials due to their high strength-to-weight ratio, corrosion resistance and recyclability, good thermal and electrical conductivity and favourable formability through rolling, extrusion, and welding [ 1 ]. These properties make them attractive for applications in automotive engines, aerospace structures, marine vessels, and defence components. However, their relatively low hardness, poor wear resistance, and lower high-temperature stability compared to steels and superalloys limit their use in high-demand service environments [ 2 ]. To address these limitations, aluminium is often reinforced with secondary materials to produce aluminium matrix composites (AMCs).

AMCs belong to the broader metal matrix composites (MMCs), in which reinforcements such as fibres, particulates, or whiskers are dispersed within a metallic matrix [ 3 ]. These reinforcements improve the load-bearing capacity by restricting dislocation motion, improving stiffness, wear, creep and fatigue behaviours [ 4 ]. The interest in AMCs lies in their potential to combine the lightweight nature of aluminium with the hardness, strength and thermal stability of the ceramic reinforcements, thereby producing hybrid materials that are suitable for demanding applications like automotive engine blocks, brake rotors, and aerospace turbine components [ 5 ,  6 ]. Reinforcements used in AMCs are broadly classified into synthetic and agro-waste categories. Conventional synthetic reinforcements include silicon carbide (SiC), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ), titanium carbide (TiC), boron carbide (B 4 C), zirconia (ZrO 2 ), and silicon nitride (Si 3 N 4 ). Nirala et al. [ 7 ] demonstrated that SiC reinforcement significantly increased hardness, density, and wear resistance, while B 4 C improved the elastic modulus and fracture toughness of aluminium alloy. Despite these benefits, synthetic ceramics are expensive and relatively dense, leading to heavier and less economically viable composites for large-scale automotive and aerospace applications.

As a result, agricultural residues such as rice husk ash, sugarcane bagasse ash, and palm kernel shell ash have been explored as potential sustainable and eco-friendly reinforcements [ 8 ,  9 ]. These wastes are rich in oxides such as silica, alumina, and iron oxide, which enable them to enhance mechanical strength, wear resistance, and thermal properties when incorporated into aluminium. Beyond performance benefits, agro-waste reinforcements provide a sustainable route to waste management, reducing environmental pollution caused by open burning or indiscriminate dumping of agricultural residues [ 10 ]. Date palm seed ash (DPSA), in particular, represents a novel and underexplored agro-waste reinforcement. With Nigeria and other West African countries among the largest consumers of date fruits, vast quantities of date seeds are discarded annually. While previous studies have examined date seeds for biofuel and biochar production, their valorisation as reinforcement in aluminium composites remains limited [ 11 ]. Importantly, DPSA is rich in iron oxide and contains silica and alumina, making it chemically suited for improving the mechanical and thermal properties of aluminium alloys [ 12 ,  13 ].

Several synthesis techniques have been developed for producing AMCs, each with distinct advantages and drawbacks. These include powder metallurgy, casting or liquid metallurgy, and additive manufacturing or 3D printing [ 14 ]. Casting remains the most widely applied method, where reinforcements are incorporated into molten aluminium and solidified. Casting is economical and versatile, but presents challenges with reinforcement clustering and interfacial bonding [ 15 ]. After synthesis, the composites undergo secondary treatments to further enhance the properties. While the choice of reinforcement and synthesis method significantly influences structural and functional performance of composites, post-processing treatments are equally important in tailoring microstructures for improved strength, ductility, toughness and thermal stability [ 16 ]. Research has shown that secondary treatments of A356-based composites enhance wear resistance, fatigue strength, and dimensional stability, which are critical factors in automotive and aerospace applications [ 17 ,  18 ]. Among the various techniques, heat treatments such as T6 treatment have been employed to strengthen aluminium-based composites by altering the precipitation behaviour of alloying elements. A study by Lu et al. [ 19 ]. showed that A356 alloys respond strongly to controlled solutionising and ageing heat treatment (T6-treatment). This was demonstrated for the casting of motorcycle wheel hubs. It was reported that T6 Treatment improved the mechanical properties of the alloy.

While there are several empirical studies on the use of agro-wastes as reinforcement materials in AMCs, there are limited studies on the secondary treatment of these composites. Vinod et al. [ 20 ]. used the double-stir casting technique to co-introduce organic RHA and inorganic fly ash into the A356 alloy to address poor wettability and agglomeration, typical of agro-ash. As-cast mechanical properties showed clear increases in hardness and some strength metrics as agro-ash proportion rose from 5 to 10 wt%. No post-casting treatment was discussed. Similarly, Mustafa et al. [ 21 ] produced hybrid AMCs by stir casting AA8011 with a fixed 2.5 wt% rice husk ash (RHA) and varying SiC content. The findings showed that increasing SiC markedly improved hardness and wear resistance, while adding RHA alone delivered only marginal tribological benefits. The RHA acted as a low-cost, partially amorphous silica filler rather than as a load-bearing ceramic. The study did not also investigate the influence of secondary treatment. Poornesh et al. [ 22 ] studied the centrifugal mould casting of Al-Si reinforced with coconut shell ash (CSA), which increased tensile strength up to 197 MPa compared to 112 MPa for the unreinforced alloy, with an optimal ash content of 7.5 wt%. The study showed that centrifugal casting plus controlled melt parameters can reduce porosity and yield grain refinement, which together boost strength. The study recommended secondary ageing treatment to further enhance the properties of the composites.

Recent studies on natural fibre and agro-based composites have shown that improved interfacial bonding, reduced defect concentration, and controlled reinforcement architecture significantly enhance the mechanical durability and structural integrity of lightweight composites for advanced engineering applications [ 23 ,  24 ]. Unlike several agro-waste reinforcements primarily rich in silica or carbonaceous phases, DPSA contains a multi-oxide composition including iron oxide, silica and magnesia with potential of improving the performance of aluminium matrix composites [ 25 ].

Despite the growing interest in agro-waste reinforced AMCs, limited studies have investigated the combined influence of DPSA reinforcement and T6 heat treatment on the thermomechanical and tribological behaviour of gravity die cast A356 composites. Furthermore, the use of calcined DPSA as a sustainable oxide-rich reinforcement in AMCs remains largely underexplored. Therefore, the present study focused on the development of gravity die cast A356/DPSA composite reinforced with varying DPSA contents and evaluated the influence of T6 treatment on their density, mechanical behaviour, wear resistance, thermal stability, coefficient of thermal expansion and microstructural evolution. The novelty of this work lies in the combined investigation of low-weight fraction DPSA reinforcement and T6 treatment in tailoring the functional performance of A356 alloy for lightweight automotive applications.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: The materials for this study are A356 alloy and Date Palm (Phoenix dactylifera) Seed Ash (DPSA). The DPSA was obtained by the calcination of Date Palm Seed (DPS) at 500 °C for 4 h. The chemical compositions of the A356 alloy and the DPSA are presented in Tables  1  and  2 . The chemical composition of the alloy was obtained by examining a 20 mm diameter by 20 mm height of the alloy in an optical electron spectroscope. With a Si content of 7.36 vol% and Al content of 91.8%, the sample alloy qualifies as an A356 alloy [ 17 ]. Meanwhile, the chemical composition of the DPSA sample was obtained with the aid of a PANalytical Epsilon 3 XRF analyser, which showed that Fe 2 O 3  (48.40 wt%), K 2 O (21.47 wt%), P 2 O 5  (7.39 wt%), CaO (5.72 wt%) and SiO 2  (5.16 wt%) were the major oxides.

sections.heading: Casting procedure
paragraphs: The composites were produced by compo-casting, which involved semi-solid incorporation of the reinforcement into the melt alloy at a temperature range of 585 –595 °C [ 26 ]. A356 alloy was melted at 750 °C and cooled to 710 °C for the addition of 1 wt% pure magnesium to improve the wettability between the DPSA particles and the molten alloy. Thereafter, the melt was further allowed to cool to 595 °C for semi-solid mixing to allow for easy dispersion of the DPSA particles due to the high viscosity of the melt [ 26 ]. An electronically operated stirrer at a stirring rate of 300 rpm was used to stir the melt until a vortex was formed. Thereafter, DPSA particles, which were preheated at 350 °C were incorporated, while stirring continued. After the addition of the reinforcement, the stirrer was left to run for 5 min to ensure uniform mixing. The temperature was then raised to 700 °C and held for 10 min before pouring into a 2-piece gravity casting die measuring 150 mm × 50 mm × 50 mm and clamped together with aid of a C-clamp, Fig.  1 a. Fig.  1 b is the produced composites. Table  3  shows the mixing ratios of the composites.

sections.heading: T6-treatment
paragraphs: Two sets of samples were prepared from the cast billet, the first represents the as-cast condition, while the second was subjected to T6 heat treatment (T6). T6 is a 2-stage heat treatment procedure that involves solutionising heat treatment and artificial ageing [ 27 ]. The solutionising heat treatment was done by holding the specimen a Nabertherm furnace (Model: B 180) heated at 540 °C for 6 h and thereafter quenching in tap water. This was followed by artificial ageing heat treatment at 160 °C in an oven for 6 h to achieve a near peak ageing condition. Thereafter, the samples were air-cooled [ 26 ].

sections.heading: Thermomechanical properties
paragraphs: All mechanical, tribological, thermal, and physical property measurements were conducted using three replicate samples under identical experimental conditions, and the reported values represent the average of the obtained results. The experimental repeatability was evaluated through standard deviation analysis to ensure the reliability and consistency of the measured data.

sections.heading: Density
Tensile and compressive tests
paragraphs: The tensile test was conducted in line with the procedure of ASTM-E8/E8M standards [ 29 ,  30 ] for round with a diameter of 12.7 mm and a 50 mm gauge length. The compressive test was performed in accordance with ASTM E9 [ 31 ]. The length and diameter of the specimen were 20 mm and 10 mm, respectively, to maintain the required aspect ratio of 2.0. Both tests were conducted using the TestTeK – 50, servo-controlled EM UTM. The tensile and compressive stress-strain curves were plotted electronically.

sections.heading: Thermogravimetric Analysis (TGA)
paragraphs: The thermal stability of the composites was evaluated using a HITACHI STA 7300 simultaneous thermal analyser. Metal chip samples were carefully prepared and placed in the sample pan. The analysis was conducted in an air atmosphere, with the temperature programmed from 30 °C to 1000 °C at a heating rate of 10 °C/min. During the heating, the change in sample mass was continuously recorded as a function of temperature and time. The thermogravimetric (TG) provided information on the onset of oxidation, rate of weight change, and thermal degradation behaviour of the composites [ 34 ].

Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM)
paragraphs: Detailed surface morphology and elemental composition were investigated using a scanning electron microscope (Zeiss EVO 18 special edition). The samples were cut to 20 mm × 20 mm × 15 mm dimensions. Initial surface preparation involved dry polishing with emery papers from 80 to 800 grit, followed by wet polishing with finer emery papers from 1000 to 2500 grit. Final polishing was performed on a cloth using diamond spray in combination with a suitable lubricant until a mirror-like surface finish was obtained. To reveal the microstructural features, the polished specimens were etched with Keller’s reagent by immersion for 2–3 s, followed by rinsing with distilled water and drying in air. The Keller’s reagent was prepared by adding 5 ml of HNO 3 , 3 ml of HCl and 2 ml of HF to 190 ml and stirring continuously with a magnetic stirrer until a clear solution is formed. The etched samples were then examined using the SEM machine.

sections.heading: Density
paragraphs: Figure  2  shows the theoretical density and the density of the as-cast and T6-treated composites. The theoretical density was calculated with the rule of mixtures [ 36 ]. Given that the density of DPSA is lower than that of aluminium, it is expected that there would be a reduction in the density of the composites with incremental addition of the reinforcement. However, experimentally, the densities of the composites were higher both in as-cast and T6-treated conditions than those of the base alloy. For the as-cast, the density ranged from 2.61 ± 0.13 g/cc in the control sample (0 wt%) to 2.65 ± 0.11 g/cc at 1.0 wt%. There was a decline from 2.63 ± 0.09 g/cc to 2.62 ± 0.13 g/cc, moving from the 0.25 wt% sample to the 0.5 wt% sample, suggesting that the 0.5 wt% sample has more pores than the other composites. Meanwhile, with a density of 2.61 ± 0.13 g/cc for 0 wt%, it can be asserted that the gravity die-cast A356 alloy is less dense and contains more pores than the composites. This shows that the addition of DPSA helped close the voids resulting from the gravity die-casting process. The densities obtained are within the range of a typical gravity die-cast aluminium alloy [ 37 ]. Meanwhile, the T6-treated density ranged from 2.60 ± 0.12 g/cc (0 wt%) to 2.65 ± 0.11 g/cc (1.0 wt%). It can be observed from Fig.  2  that the densities of the T6-treated samples were lower than their corresponding As-cast densities up to 0.5 wt%, which recorded the same value of density (2.61 ± 0.12 g/cc) for both conditions. The density of T6-treated 0.75 wt% (2.64 ± 0.11 g/cc) was slightly higher than the corresponding as-cast density (2.63 ± 0.11 g/cc). The same value of density was recorded for the as-cast and T6-treated 1.0 wt% reinforcement. This is because T6-treatment can open up micro-shrinkage pores and allow dissolved gases to expand upon quenching, resulting in the low densities recorded at low reinforcement loading [ 38 ]. This behaviour is inhibited as the quantity of DPSA particles increases at higher loading. Overall, T6 treatment did not inherently increase density across all formulations; rather, it elaborated the effect of reinforcement on densification. This aligns with the findings of Edosa et al. [ 39 ]., who opined that T6-treatment leads to a decrease in composite densities.
Fig. 2 Density of gravity die cast samples

Although the theoretical density decreased slightly with increasing DPSA addition due to the lower density of DPSA relative to that of the Aluminium matrix, the experimental density exhibited a gradual increase. This behaviour may be attributed to the improved matrix compactness, enhanced particle-assisted packing efficiency, and reduced casting porosity at low reinforcement loadings, which outweighed the effect of the lower-density reinforcement. Similar increase in density of AMCs despite the use of low-density reinforcement has been reported in previous studies [ 39 ,  40 ].

The slightly higher experimental densities of the composites compared to the base alloy suggest improvement in the matrix compactness and reduction in the effective porosity at intermediate DPSA loadings. This may be attributed to improved particle-assisted packing and better interdendritic filling during solidification. While, the T6-treated samples had lower densities than the as-cast, the T6-treated composites also showed higher densities than the T6-treated pure A356 alloy. The reduction in densities of the T6-treated samples can be associated with the opening or expansion of pre-existing micropores during solutionising and quenching, which is common in gravity-cast aluminium alloys [ 41 ].

sections.heading: Tensile strength
paragraphs: The stress-strain curves for the as-cast samples are presented in Fig.  4 a. It can be observed that all reinforced samples demonstrated higher tensile strength than the base alloy. The UTS ranged from 162.0 ± 8.1 MPa in the 0 wt% sample to 193.1 ± 9.7 MPa in the 0.75 wt% sample. The UTS of 0.25 wt%, 0.5 wt% and 1.0 wt% are 190.0 ± 9.5 MPa, 179.1 ± 9.0 MPa and 166.9 ± 8.3 MPa respectively. The increase in the UTS of the reinforced samples can be attributed to the load-bearing effect of the oxide-rich DPSA particles. Meanwhile, the pure A356 alloy showed the highest elongation (7.4 ± 0.4%). The elongation decreased with increased reinforcement level, as the elongations for 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, and 1.0 wt% samples are 6.2 ± 0.3%, 5.6 ± 0.3%, 5.6 ± 0.3% and 4.9 ± 0.2%, respectively. The reduction in %elongation shows that the composites are less ductile than the base alloy, which is typical of a ceramic or agro-waste reinforced metal matrix composite. The reduction in ductility could be due to the formation of micro-voids around the DPSA particles during tensile loading. The 0.75 wt% composite has the highest UTS among the samples, which suggests an optimal balance of good particle dispersion, sufficient reinforcement for load transfer and moderate levels of casting porosity as seen in the density test results.

Figure  4 b displays the tensile stress-strain curves for the T6-treated samples produced by gravity die casting. It is observed that the UTS ranged from 182.1 ± 9.1 MPa (0 wt%) to 292.7 ± 14.6 MPa (0.75 wt%). The UTS for the other compositions are 185.0 ± 9.2 MPa (0.25 wt%), 240.9 ± 12.0 MPa (0.5 wt%), and 277.9 ± 13.9 MPa (1.0 wt%). Similarly, the values of percentage elongation for the various compositions are 8.8 ± 0.4 (0 wt%), 6.1 ± 0.3 (0.25 wt%), 5.6 ± 0.3 (0.5 wt%), 6.6 ± 0.3 (0.75 wt%), and 6.2 ± 0.3 (1.0 wt%). It can be observed that T6-treatment improved the UTS and %elongation of the composites. The combined effect of T6 treatment and DPSA reinforcement roughly increased UTS by 37% over the T6-treated A356 (0 wt%), with an optimum at 0.75 wt% DPSA. The increase in elongation after T6 treatment may be attributed to the spheroidisation and fragmentation of the eutectic Si particles. The transformation of the coarse acicular Si morphology into rounded particles reduced stress concentration sites within the matrix, thereby improving strain accommodation and ductility.

The findings of the study align with those of Aigbodion [ 42 ], who observed a 35% increase in tensile strength of Al-Cu-Mg/Bean pod composite, however, it required 4 wt% reinforcement to achieve this result as compared to 0.75 wt% DPSA as recorded in this study. Similarly, Mu et al. [ 43 ]. reported improvement in the UTS of SiC/AA2024 composites after T6 treatment. There was also a noticeable improvement in the percentage elongation. The strengthening mechanism can be attributed to the formation of Mg 2 Si during precipitation hardening and load transfer from DPSA particles, as well as the modification of the grain size and texture of the microstructure [ 39 ]. The drop in UTS at 1.0 wt% can be attributed to the onset of clustering and an increase in microvoid population, which were also observed in the tensile data of the as-cast composites (Fig.  3 ).
Fig. 3 Tensile stress-strain curve ( a ) As-cast ( b ) T6-treated

sections.heading: Compressive strength
paragraphs: Figure  4 a shows the compressive stress-strain curve for the composites. By visual inspection, it is observed that all the reinforced composites outperformed the pure A356 sample. The compressive strength (CS) ranged from 178 ± 8.9 MPa at 0 wt% to 263 ± 13.2 MPa at 0.5 wt%. The CS for 0.25, 0.75, and 1.0 wt% samples are 232 ± 11.6 MPa, 255 ± 12.7 MPa and 252 ± 12.6 MPa, respectively. The increase in the CS of the composites can be attributed to the rigid load-bearing capacity of the DPSA particles, resisting the matrix deformation. The 0.5 wt% sample achieved the highest compressive strength. At higher loading, reinforcements tend to cluster in gravity casting, leading to particle-particle interference and the clustering of microvoids, which results in the reduced CS for 0.75 wt% and 1.0 wt% samples.
Fig. 4 Compressive strength for gravity die cast samples ( a )As-cast ( b )T6-treated

The compressive stress-strain graphs for the T6-treated samples are presented in Fig.  4 b. The compressive yield strength varied from 280 ± 14.0 MPa (0 wt%) to 302 ± 15.1 MPa (0.75 wt%). The compressive yield strengths for the other compositions are 300 ± 15.0 MPa (0.25 wt%), 296 ± 14.8 MPa (0.5 wt%) and 285 ± 14.3 MPa (1.0 wt%). The results revealed a substantial increase in the compressive strength for all the reinforced samples compared with the unreinforced alloy. 0.75 wt% showed the highest compressive strength, closely followed by 0.25 wt%. The enhancement in compressive strength is attributed to the combined effects of precipitation hardening and load-bearing capacity of the DPSA particles, which provide strong constraints on plastic flow under compressive loading [ 44 ].

sections.heading: Hardness
paragraphs: The hardness behaviour of the as-cast and T6-treated composites is presented in Fig.  5 . Figure  5 a shows the Brinell Hardness Number (HBN) of the as-cast composites varied from 57.6 ± 2.5 HBN in the control sample (0 wt%) to 70.2 ± 4.5 HBN at 0.75 wt% reinforcement, representing a 23% improvement. The hardness values of 0.25 wt%, 0.5 wt% and 1.0 wt% are 59.6 ± 2.9 HBN, 65.8 ± 4.4 HBN, and 60.2 ± 2.8 HBN, respectively. Meanwhile, the HBN of the T6-treated composites varied from 87.8 ± 2.7 HBN (0 wt%) to 113.6 ± 1.6 HBN (1.0 wt%). The hardness values for 0.25, 0.5, and 0.75 wt% are 100.5 ± 5.9 HBN, 94.5 ± 10.0 HBN, and 108.2 ± 3.9 HBN, respectively.
Fig. 5 Hardness of gravity die cast samples ( a ) HBN ( b ) Vickers microhardness

Similarly, Fig.  5 b displays the microhardness of the samples measured in HV. The microhardness of the as-cast composites ranged from 70.6 ± 4.0 HV at 0 wt% to 89.2 ± 1.6 HV at 0.75 wt%, representing an increase of 27%. The other composites: 0.25 wt%, 0.5 wt% and 1.0 wt% recorded 72.4 ± 4.0 HV, 79.6 ± 4.6 HV and 72.28 ± 3.5 HV, respectively. After T6-treatment, the results revealed that the microhardness values of the composites are 98.8 ± 1.2 HV (0 wt%), 108.1 ± 5.5 HV (0.25 wt%), 138.2 ± 1.1 HV (0.5 wt%), 122.3 ± 5.2 HV (0.75 wt%) and 126.7 ± 4.0 HV (1.0 wt%). The hardness results showed that while Brinell hardness improved from 0 wt% to 1.0 wt%, Vickers’ microhardness peaked at 0.5 wt%, then experienced a decline at 0.75 wt% before a recovery at 1.0 wt%. The difference in the two hardness tests results at higher reinforcement levels showed that while bulk resistance to indentation continues to improve, local heterogeneities increasingly control micro-scale deformation [ 45 ,  46 ]. The combined hardness results therefore confirm that 0.5 wt% DPSA represents the optimal micro-mechanical condition, whereas 0.75-1.0 wt% favours macro-scale stiffness and wear resistance after T6 treatment.

sections.heading: Wear behaviour
paragraphs: The wear behaviour of the composites is measured in terms of wear rate and coefficient of friction (CoF) as shown in Fig.  6 . The wear rate of the as-cast composites (Fig.  6 a) witnessed small reductions from 0 wt% (7.8 ± 0.7 × 10 − 6  g/s) to 0.75 wt% (7.35 ± 0.4 × 10 − 6  g/s), then a sharp increase at 1.0 wt% (9.0 ± 0.7 × 10 − 6  g/s). Similarly, the CoF falls from 0 wt% (0.42 ± 0.18) to 0.75 wt% (0.37 ± 0.06) and then rises to 1.0 wt% (0.45 ± 0.05). The improvement in wear behaviour up to 0.75 wt% reinforcement can be attributed to the presence of hard-phase reinforcement [ 47 ]. DPSA particles are hard and increase the surface hardness (as seen from the hardness test results), which resists adhesive wear, leading to reduced mass loss. Furthermore, it can be asserted that at moderate reinforcement, the oxide films can form a stable tribofilm that reduces metal-metal contact [ 48 ], which explains the reduction in CoF up to 0.75 wt%. The sharp increase in the wear rate and CoF at 1.0 wt% can be attributed to particle agglomeration and pull-out. At high reinforcement loading, gravity casting tends to promote clusters and weak interfaces, leading to particle detachment that accelerates abrasive wear.
Fig. 6 Wear behaviour of gravity die-cast samples ( a ) As-cast ( b ) T6-treated

The wear behaviour of the T6-treated composites is presented in Fig.  6 b. The wear rate varied from 42.3 ± 2.1 × 10 − 6  g/s (0 wt%) to 6.6 ± 0.3 × 10 − 6  g/s (0.75 wt%). The wear rates of the other compositions are 11.7 ± 0.6 × 10 − 6  g/s (0.25 wt%), 8.4 ± 0.4 × 10 − 6  g/s (0.5 wt%), and 8.5 ± 0.4 × 10 − 6  g/s (1.0 wt%). Meanwhile, the CoF increased from 0.35 ± 0.08 (0 wt%) to 0.57 ± 0.11 (1.0 wt%). The CoF of the intermediary compositions are 0.585 ± 0.42 (0.25 wt%), 0.42 ± 0.46 (0.5 wt%), and 0.45 ± 0.04 (0.75 wt%).

These results showed that the wear behaviour of the T6-treated gravity die cast A356/DPSA composites strongly depends on reinforcement fraction. The unreinforced alloy exhibits the highest wear rate due to its relatively low hardness. The introduction of DPSA significantly reduces wear rate by providing hard oxide-rich particles that increase surface hardness. The minimum wear rate is observed at 0.75 wt% DPSA, where reinforcement loading and particle dispersion are optimum, yielding a stable tribolayer and moderate coefficient of friction [ 49 ]. At 1.0 wt% DPSA, particle clustering and microvoids lead to fracture and pull-out of reinforcement particles, resulting in third-body abrasion, thereby increasing the CoF and causing a slight rise in wear rate despite the high hardness [ 50 ]. Based on the wear behaviour, the 0.75 wt% T6-treated sample is considered the optimum composition for gravity die casting.

The improved wear resistance at intermediate DPSA loading is associated with enhanced surface hardness and the formation of a more stable tribolayer, whereas excessive reinforcement promoted particle pull-out and third-body abrasion, leading to increased wear deterioration at higher reinforcement levels [ 51 ].

sections.heading: XRD spectra
paragraphs: Fig. 7 XRD spectra ( a ) DPSA sample ( b ) As-cast composites ( b )T6-treated composites

Although the peak positions remained constant, the intensities of Al and Si peaks varied noticeably across 0–1.0 wt% reinforcement. This variation is valuable because changing intensity leads to microstructural evolution, in terms of crystallographic texture and interface strain. In the 0 wt% sample, the Al (111) and the (220) are the sharpest peaks; these peaks were reduced with increased addition of DPSA, except in the 0.5 wt% sample, where the Al (111) peak was very intense, and in the 1.0 wt% where the Al (220) peak had the highest intensity. At 0.75 wt%, it is observed that the Al (111) and Al (200) peaks have equal intensity. Aligning this with the mechanical properties observed from tensile, compressive, and hardness tests, it can be asserted that the growth of the Al (200) peak is responsible for the improved mechanical properties. A slight decrease in mechanical properties was observed at 1.0 wt%, where the Al (220) peak was similar to that of the base metal. This shows that clustering of particles led to the alignment of grains along the Al (220) plane. Another key observation from the XRD patterns is that the spectrum of 0.75 wt% shows equal peak intensity across major peaks, indicating more uniform columnar grains. This explains why 0.75 wt% showed a better combination of the properties.

sections.heading: Thermogravimetric analysis
paragraphs: The TGA of the as-cast samples is presented in Fig.  8 a. It is observed that the unreinforced A356 (0 wt%) sample exhibited the largest net mass loss on heating, falling to about 96.0% at 800 °C before reversing and rising towards 98.5% at 1000 °C due to oxidation of aluminium. Meanwhile, the DPSA-reinforced samples (0.25–1.0 wt%) showed much smaller net mass losses over 25–700 °C (0.2–1.5% loss), and displayed mass gain due to oxidation beginning at 750–850 °C. It is observed that the reinforcement stabilises mass up to mid-temperatures (> 800 °C), beyond this point, all samples began to show oxide-scale growth, but the timing and magnitude varied with the DPSA content.
Fig. 8 TGA curves for gravity die cast samples ( a ) As-cast ( b ) T6-treated

A critical analysis of the thermal degradation at different temperatures showed that from room temperature to about 300 °C, there was a small decrease in mass of all samples. This is likely due to the removal of adsorbed moisture, surface contaminants and any loosely bound residues [ 55 ]. Between 200 and 700 °C, there was slow but progressive mass loss, which was much larger in the unreinforced A356. The possible contributors to this phenomenon may include the decomposition of low-level contaminants, including carbonaceous residue that may be present in the reinforcement. However, it is observed that the loss in mass is less for the composites compared to the control, indicating that the DPSA is largely inert. Another reason could be the oxidation of minor alloying elements that may be present in the alloy, such as Mg [ 56 ]. The presence of porosity can also foster mass loss. Porosity is a common feature of gravity cast alloys. However, the addition of DPSA seemed to reduce the porosity, hence the improved thermal behaviour. Between 750 and 1000 °C, reversal to mass again was observed in all samples. The upward turn is characteristic of oxygen uptake and oxide-scale growth, mainly due to the change of Al to Al 2 O 3  [ 34 ]. The temperature at which the trend reverses and the slope of mass increase differed by composition. Reinforced samples showed the onset of mass gain at slightly lower or similar temperatures, but with different magnitudes. This can be attributed to the oxide constituents of the DPSA particles and the particle-matrix interfaces that modify the oxidation kinetics. The reversal occurred later in the unreinforced sample but at a larger slope, which suggests the formation of oxide scales, but spallation or prior mass loss dominates until very high temperatures. The practical application is that for automotive engine components, the reinforced gravity-die cast composites with low DPSA (0.25–0.75 wt%) show acceptable thermal stability below 500 °C.

The TGA curves of the T6-treated gravity die cast samples are presented in Fig.  8 b. Compared with the as-cast condition, the unreinforced A356 alloy exhibited slightly lower weight loss after T6 treatment, whereas the T6-treated DPSA-reinforced composites showed higher weight loss than their corresponding as-cast counterparts. This behaviour is attributed to the thermal decomposition of metastable and unstable intermetallic phases formed at the matrix–DPSA interfaces during the solution and ageing stages of the T6 heat treatment [ 39 ]. Nevertheless, the reinforced composites remained more thermally stable than the monolithic A356 alloy, with the 0.75 wt% and 0.25 wt% DPSA samples exhibiting the best overall thermal stability.

sections.heading: CTE
paragraphs: Fig. 9 CTE for gravity die cast samples ( a ) As-cast ( b ) T6-treated

After T6 treatment (Fig.  9 b), all samples retained the same temperature-dependent trend, but the CTE values were lower than those of the corresponding as-cast samples. The CTE for the control sample (0 wt%) increased from 13.69 × 10 − 6  /K to 19.93 × 10 − 6  /K, while for 0.25 wt%, the CTE increased from 10.56 × 10 − 6  /K to 17.87 × 10 − 6  /K, and from 10.38 × 10 − 6  /K to 18.34 × 10 − 6  /K for 0.5 wt%. The CTE for 0.75 wt% increased from 10.36 × 10 − 6  /K to 18.4 × 10 − 6  /K, and for 1.0 wt%, it increased from 11.5 × 10 − 6  /K to 18.95 × 10 − 6  /K. This shows that T6 reduces CTE by enhancing interfacial bonding, which aids thermal load transfer. Across the full temperature range, the lowest CTE is consistently observed at 0.25–0.75 wt%, showing that moderate reinforcement is most effective for suppressing expansion in gravity-cast aluminium composites.

The reduction in CCTE is primarily due to thermal mismatch between the thermally stable oxide-rich DPSA particles and the A356 matrix, which restrict the matrix expansion during heating. In addition, the oxide constituents of DPSA contributed to improved oxidation resistance by forming more stable protective layers at elevated temperatures, thereby reducing thermal degradation and mass loss [ 60 ].

sections.heading: Microstructural analysis
paragraphs: Fig. 10 SEM images of as-cast composites at 1.5 kx magnification ( a ) 0 wt% ( b ) 0.25 wt% ( c ) 0.5 wt% ( d ) 0.75 wt% ( e ) 1.0 wt%
Fig. 11 SEM images of T6-treated composites at 1.5 kx magnification ( a ) 0 wt% ( b ) 0.25 wt% ( c ) 0.5 wt% ( d ) 0.75 wt% ( e ) 1.0 wt%

The SEM micrographs of T6-treated composites are presented in Fig.  11 a–e. The microstructure of the 0T6 (Fig.  11 a) appears to be relatively smooth and continuous. Dark interdendritic regions associated with spheroidised eutectic Si and localised microvoids are observable. The variations in contrast are mainly due to precipitated Mg 2 Si and spheroidised Si [ 62 ]. These precipitates contribute to precipitation strengthening, while the spheroidization of eutectic Si reduces stress concentration within the matrix. These residual micro-voids act as crack initiation sites under tensile and impact loading and create easy pathways for oxidative attack during TGA [ 63 ]. With the addition of DPSA in 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1.0 wt%, localised pore-like defects and interdendritic regions appeared less pronounced. The optimum microstructure is observed in samples between 0.5 and 0.75 wt% with a compact, defect-controlled microstructure. Particle imprints are evenly spaced, indicating optimal dispersion, which supports efficient load transfer and strong particle-matrix interfacial bonding. The improved hardness and strength after T6 treatment suggest that DPSA particles may have influenced precipitate distribution and matrix strengthening during ageing. This is further supported by the variation in the distribution of the eutectic Si phase across the various compositions.

The observed microstructural refinement at intermediate DPSA loadings, particularly at 0.75 wt%, significantly contributed to the enhanced mechanical and tribological performance of the composites. The finer and more uniformly distributed interdendritic features promoted improved load transfer, restricted plastic deformation, and enhanced wear resistance. However, the presence of particle agglomeration and localised defects at 1.0 wt% DPSA contributed to stress concentration, which explains the reduction in mechanical and tribological performance at this composition. Furthermore, the microstructural evolution was strongly influenced by the processing conditions. The choice of compo-casting through semi-solid mixing improved wettability and dispersion of DPSA particles within the A356 matrix, leading to refined interdendritic features. However, excessive DPSA addition promoted particle agglomeration due to increased particle-to-particle interaction and reduced melt flowability during casting. However, T6 treatment modified the eutectic Si morphology and enhanced interfacial bonding, contributing to the improved thermomechanical and tribological behaviour of the composites.

Comparative measurements obtained from the SEM micrographs in Fig.  12  revealed noticeable changes in the characteristic interdendritic feature dimensions with DPSA addition and T6 treatment. In the as-cast condition, the unreinforced alloy (Fig.  12 a) exhibited coarser interdendritic features with dimensions ranging approximately from 34 to 47 μm. Meanwhile, 0.75 wt% DPSA composite (Fig.  12 b) showed finer and more compact features ranging from about 12–24 μm, indicating microstructural refinement and improved phase distribution. After T6 treatment, the microstructure became smoother and more spheroidised due to diffusion-driven modification of the eutectic Si phase. Although slightly larger feature dimensions were observed in the T6-treated samples, the 0.75T6 composite (Fig.  12 d) still exhibited a more refined and uniformly distributed microstructure than the unreinforced 0T6 sample. The detailed interdendritic measurement for all compositions is presented in Table  4 . The results demonstrate a strong relationship between microstructural refinement and the optimum thermomechanical and tribological performance obtaomed at 0.75 wt% DPSA reinforcement.

sections.heading: Comparative summary of thermomechanical and tribological properties
paragraphs: Table  5  highlights the beneficial influence of T6 treatment on the thermomechanical and tribological properties of the developed composites by comparing the best values obtained for each material property in As-cast and T6-treated conditions. The heat-treated composites exhibited substantial improvements in tensile and compressive strength, Brinell hardness, and Vickers hardness. These improvements are associated with precipitation strengthening following solution treatment and artificial ageing. Furthermore, the reduction in wear rate after T6 treatment indicates improved surface resistance to material removal during sliding. Although only a slight reduction in CTE was observed, the improved dimensional stability remains beneficial for lightweight automotive components exposed to thermal cycling.

Table  6  compares the performance of the developed DPSA-reinforced composites with related agro-waste reinforced aluminium matrix composites reported in literature. Compared with previous studies, the present study achieved significantly higher improvements in tensile strength and hardness at a substantially lower reinforcement loading of only 0.75 wt%. This behaviour highlights the effectiveness of the combined influence of the oxide-rich DPSA reinforcement, improved particle dispersion, and T6 treatment in enhancing matrix strengthening and structural stability. Furthermore, unlike many previous studies based solely on stir casting, the use of compocasting and gravity die casting contributed to improved structural integrity of the composite.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: The present study demonstrated the development of gravity die-cast A356/DPSA composites for automotive applications. DPSA addition in small amounts of 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1.0 wt% and T6 treatment significantly influenced the thermomechanical, tribological, thermal and microstructural behaviour of the composites. The optimum combination of these properties was obtained at 0.75 wt% DPSA, which exhibited improved tensile strength, compressive strength, hardness, wear resistance and thermal stability. The as-cast and T6-treated composites showed refined α-Al dendritic structure and a more uniformly distributed eutectic Si network at intermediate DPSA loadings. Excessive reinforcement content promoted particle agglomeration and localised defects. T6 treatment further enhanced the performance of the composites through improved matrix strengthening and microstructural uniformity. The addition of DPSA to A356 led to over 37% increase in tensile strength, 29.38% increase in hardness and a reduction of 5.77% in wear rate. The developed composites are suitable for lightweight automotive engine components requiring a good combination of strength, wear resistance and thermal stability.
